explanations.Wordsworth: An English Romantic poet, who wrote Lyrical Ballads with Coleridge.
explanations.Baudelaire: A French poet, who also worked as an essayist and critic.
explanations.Rilke: A poet writing in German, and the leftover poem cell is his.
explanations.Dickens: An English novelist of the Victorian age.
explanations.Victor Hugo: The French author of Les Misérables, which puts him in the novel cell.
explanations.Thomas Mann: A German novelist, writing in German.
explanations.Tom Stoppard: A British playwright, writing in English.
explanations.Moliere: A French playwright, whose comedies are in verse.
explanations.Bertolt Brecht: A German playwright, and a poet besides.

sources.excerpt: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, helped to launch the Romantic Age in English literature with their joint publication Lyrical Ballads (1798).
Charles John Huffam Dickens was an English writer and journalist.
He created some of literature's best-known fictional characters, and is regarded by many as the greatest novelist of the Victorian era.
Sir Tom Stoppard was a British playwright and screenwriter.
Charles-Pierre Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator and art critic.
Victor-Marie Hugo, vicomte Hugo was a French Romantic author, poet, essayist, playwright, journalist, human rights activist and politician.
Les Misérables is a French epic historical novel by Victor Hugo, first published on 31 March 1862, that is considered one of the greatest novels of the 19th century.
Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, known by his stage name Molière, was a French playwright, actor, and poet, widely regarded as one of the great writers in the French language and world literature.
René Karl Wilhelm Johann Josef Maria Rilke, known as Rainer Maria Rilke, was an Austrian poet.
Acclaimed as an idiosyncratic and expressive poet, he is widely recognized as a significant writer in the German language.
His writings include one novel, several collections of poetry, several volumes of correspondence and a few early novellas.
Paul Thomas Mann was a German novelist, short story writer, social critic, philanthropist, essayist, and the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature laureate.
Eugen Berthold Friedrich Brecht, known as Bertolt Brecht and Bert Brecht, was a German theatre practitioner, playwright, and poet.

editorNotes: Victor Hugo is the intended overlap and he is kept, not replaced: his page names him as a poet and a playwright, and Les Misérables makes him a novelist, so he truly fits all three French cells. The matching still comes out single. The French novel cell is the only cell Hugo alone can fill, since Baudelaire is a poet and critic and Molière a man of the theatre, so Hugo is pinned there; Baudelaire then fits nothing but the French poem cell, which leaves the French playwright cell to Molière. Molière is a second, smaller overlap, because his page calls him a poet as well as a playwright. The German column works the same way: Rilke wrote one novel, so he fits both the poet and the novelist cells, and Brecht is named as playwright and poet, so he fits both the poet and the playwright cells. Brecht alone can take the German playwright cell, which then sends Rilke to the poet cell and Thomas Mann, a novelist only, to the novel cell. In the English column each writer fits one cell: Wordsworth wrote a single early verse play, The Borderers, but he is named simply as a poet and no one calls him a playwright; Dickens wrote novels and journalism, not verse or plays; Stoppard wrote for stage and screen but published no poems or novels. Oscar Wilde was the first candidate for the English playwright and was dropped, because he wrote poems and a novel too and would have fitted all three English cells, leaving more than one matching.
